title: Design a Web Crawler
description: A distributed crawler that discovers, fetches, and extracts text from 10 billion web pages within 5 days while respecting robots.txt and never losing progress.

functional: Operators seed the crawler with an initial list of URLs, and it discovers new pages automatically by following outbound links
The crawler extracts and stores the clean text content of every page it visits for downstream processing (e.g. LLM training)
Already-visited URLs and duplicate content are detected and skipped so the same page is never fetched or stored twice
Crawling automatically respects each site's robots.txt rules, including the Crawl-delay directive
nonFunctional: Fault tolerance — a crashed worker or a failed fetch never loses crawl progress; work resumes from the last known state
Politeness — no more than ~1 request per second per domain, so target servers are never overloaded
Efficiency — crawl 10 billion pages to completion in under 5 days
Scalability — the fetch and parse tiers scale horizontally and independently as queue depth grows

estimates.label: Pages to crawl
estimates.note: the entire crawl must complete inside the 5-day window

estimates.label: Time budget
estimates.note: ≈ 432,000 seconds to discover and fetch every page

estimates.label: Avg. page size
estimates.note: includes embedded resources counted toward transfer bandwidth

estimates.label: Required throughput
estimates.note: 10B pages ÷ 432,000s — the floor every downstream tier must sustain

estimates.label: Fetcher fleet size
estimates.note: network-optimized instances at ~30% practical utilization of a 200 Gbps NIC

estimates.label: Per-domain limit
estimates.note: a politeness ceiling enforced independently of total fleet throughput

nodes.name: Seed URL Source
nodes.details:
### Responsibilities

- Supplies the initial list of seed URLs that bootstraps a crawl (e.g. a curated list of top domains)
- Can also inject high-priority URLs mid-crawl for freshness-sensitive re-crawls
- Not itself part of the crawl loop — after the first batch, all new URLs are discovered by the Parser and re-queued automatically

nodes.name: Frontier Queue
nodes.details:
### Responsibilities

- Holds every URL waiting to be fetched, decoupling URL discovery from fetch capacity
- Uses SQS visibility timeouts so a crashed worker's message automatically reappears instead of being lost
- Tracks `ApproximateReceiveCount` per message to drive exponential backoff and eventual dead-lettering

### Why not a plain in-memory queue

At 10B URLs the frontier itself is a distributed, durable data structure — it must survive fetcher crashes and restarts without losing the crawl's place.

nodes.name: Dead Letter Queue
nodes.details:
### Responsibilities

- Receives messages the Frontier Queue redrives after `ApproximateReceiveCount` exceeds 5
- Isolates persistently broken URLs (dead domains, malformed pages) so they stop consuming fetcher capacity
- Reviewed by the Monitoring service — sustained DLQ growth signals a systemic problem (e.g. a misbehaving domain or a parser bug), not just one-off bad URLs

nodes.name: URL Fetcher
nodes.details:
### Responsibilities

- Dequeues a URL from the Frontier Queue and checks the per-domain rate limiter before making any request
- Resolves the domain via the DNS Resolver, then issues the HTTP GET against the target server
- Sends an HTTP HEAD first to check `Content-Length`, skipping anything over the size threshold (e.g. 10MB)
- Writes the raw HTML to blob storage, updates the URL's status in the Metadata DB, then enqueues a lightweight reference onto the Further Processing Queue — never the HTML payload itself

### Fault tolerance

Each of these is a separable step. If the process crashes before enqueueing the reference, the message simply becomes visible again in the Frontier Queue and the fetch is retried — cheap, because the DNS and blob storage calls are idempotent.

nodes.name: Politeness Rate Limiter
nodes.details:
### Responsibilities

- Holds a per-domain lock with TTL equal to that domain's `Crawl-delay` (default 1 request/second)
- Implements a distributed sliding-window counter so *all* fetcher hosts — not just one — respect the same per-domain ceiling
- Caches each domain's parsed robots.txt rules (refreshed periodically from the Metadata DB) so the hot path never blocks on a database read

### Why Redis

Politeness is a global constraint — two fetcher hosts crawling the same domain concurrently must share state, or they'll jointly exceed the 1 req/s ceiling even if each individually respects it.

nodes.name: DNS Resolver
nodes.details:
### Responsibilities

- Resolves each target domain to an IP address before the fetcher opens a connection
- Caches resolutions locally per fetcher host, since DNS lookups have historically consumed up to 70% of a naive crawler thread's elapsed time
- Round-robins across multiple upstream resolvers to avoid any single resolver becoming a bottleneck at crawl scale

nodes.name: Target Web Servers
nodes.details: Represents the millions of independent domains across the public internet that the crawler fetches from. Every request against this node is bound by that domain's robots.txt rules and rate limit — this is the boundary the Politeness Rate Limiter exists to protect.

nodes.name: Further Processing Queue
nodes.details:
### Responsibilities

- Carries a lightweight reference (URL id + blob storage location) for every successfully fetched page, never the HTML itself
- Decouples fetch throughput from parse throughput — the two tiers scale independently based on their own queue depth
- Parser worker autoscaling is driven directly off this queue's depth metric

nodes.name: Raw HTML Storage
nodes.details:
### Responsibilities

- Stores the raw HTML fetched for every URL, keyed by URL/crawl id
- Decouples the fetch stage from the parse stage — the Further Processing Queue carries only a reference, so parser workers pull HTML from here rather than from the queue payload
- Kept even after parsing so text-extraction logic can be improved and re-run later without re-fetching — bandwidth, not storage, is the scarce resource

nodes.name: Monitoring & Alerting
nodes.details:
### Responsibilities

- Tracks Frontier and Further Processing Queue depth as the primary signal of whether fetch/parse capacity is keeping pace
- Alerts when Dead Letter Queue growth accelerates, which usually means a systemic issue rather than isolated bad URLs
- Surfaces per-stage health (fetcher error rate, parser lag) so operators can tell *which* pipeline stage is falling behind before it threatens the 5-day deadline

nodes.name: Text & URL Extraction
nodes.details:
### Responsibilities

- Reads raw HTML from blob storage using the reference off the Further Processing Queue
- Extracts clean text and writes it to Extracted Text Storage
- Extracts outbound links, computes a content hash for dedup, and updates the URL's status and depth in the Metadata DB
- Forwards every newly discovered URL to the Dedup Filter before it's allowed back onto the Frontier Queue

### Scaling

Parsing is CPU-bound, unlike the I/O-bound fetch stage, so this tier runs on ECS Fargate / Lambda and autoscales on Further Processing Queue depth rather than on a fixed fleet size.

nodes.name: Crawl Metadata DB
nodes.details:
### Schema

**URL table** (partition key: `urlHash`)

- `status` — pending / crawled / failed
- `htmlLocation`, `textLocation` — pointers into blob storage
- `contentHash` (indexed) — for content-level dedup
- `depth` — hops from the nearest seed URL, used for crawler-trap cutoff
- `lastCrawledAt`

**Domain table** (partition key: `domain`)

- `robotsRules`, `crawlDelay`
- `lastCrawledAt` — feeds the URL Scheduler's re-crawl heuristic

nodes.name: URL Scheduler
nodes.details:
### Responsibilities

- Periodically scans the Metadata DB for pages that are stale (past their `lastCrawledAt` plus a freshness window) or high-popularity
- Re-enqueues those URLs onto the Frontier Queue so the corpus stays current between full crawls (e.g. monthly retraining cycles)
- Runs independently of the main crawl loop — it only ever *adds* work, never blocks the fetch/parse pipeline

nodes.name: URL Dedup Filter
nodes.details:
### Responsibilities

- Runs every newly extracted URL through a RedisBloom filter before it's allowed back onto the Frontier Queue
- Rejects the vast majority of already-seen URLs in O(1) with no Metadata DB round trip
- A positive match still falls through to a Metadata DB check — the bloom filter's false positives just mean a few duplicate lookups, never a missed page

### Content-level dedup

Separately, the Parser's content hash catches pages that are byte-identical under different URLs (mirrors, tracking-parameter variants) — the Bloom filter only prevents re-*crawling* the same URL, not re-*storing* the same content.

nodes.name: Extracted Text Storage
nodes.details:
### Responsibilities

- Stores the plain text extracted from each page — the actual deliverable of the crawl, ready for downstream training or processing
- Kept separate from raw HTML storage so downstream consumers never need to re-parse HTML themselves
- Organized so the 5-day crawl's output is available as a complete, addressable corpus the moment the frontier drains

flows.title: Fetch & Store a Page
flows.description: From dequeuing a URL to the raw page being durably stored.

steps.text: A fetcher worker dequeues the next URL from the Frontier Queue. The message stays invisible to other workers until it's explicitly deleted, so a crash here simply returns the URL to the queue.

Before making any request, the worker checks the Politeness Rate Limiter for a per-domain lock. If another worker is already crawling this domain within its crawl-delay window, the fetch is deferred rather than dropped.
The worker resolves the domain to an IP via the DNS Resolver. Cached resolutions avoid re-paying a lookup that historically dominated crawler thread time.
The worker issues an HTTP HEAD to check content size, then a GET to fetch the HTML from the target server.
The raw HTML is written to blob storage and the URL's status flips to 'crawled' in the Metadata DB — two idempotent operations that can each be safely retried.
Only after storage succeeds does the worker enqueue a lightweight reference — not the HTML — onto the Further Processing Queue, and finally deletes the original Frontier Queue message.

flows.title: Parse, Extract & Rejoin the Frontier
flows.description: From a fetched-page reference to newly discovered URLs re-entering the crawl.

steps.text: A parser worker dequeues a reference from the Further Processing Queue. This tier autoscales independently of the fetch tier, based purely on this queue's depth.
The worker reads the raw HTML from blob storage using the reference — the queue message was only ever a pointer.
Clean text is extracted from the HTML and written to Extracted Text Storage — the actual deliverable of the crawl.
A content hash is computed and the URL's record in the Metadata DB is updated — this hash is what catches duplicate content published under different URLs.
Every outbound link found on the page is sent to the URL Dedup Filter before it's considered for re-crawling.
The Bloom filter rejects already-seen URLs in O(1). Its rare false positives fall through to a Metadata DB check, which is authoritative but far too slow to run on every candidate.
URLs confirmed unique are pushed back onto the Frontier Queue, closing the loop that lets the crawl expand outward from the original seed list.

flows.title: Handle a Failed Fetch
flows.description: How the pipeline survives a bad domain without losing the rest of the crawl.

steps.text: A fetch attempt times out or the target server returns a 5xx error.

Because the worker never deleted the Frontier Queue message, its visibility timeout expires and the URL automatically reappears for another worker to retry, with exponential backoff driven by ApproximateReceiveCount.
After 5 failed attempts, the Frontier Queue redrives the message to the Dead Letter Queue instead of retrying indefinitely.
Monitoring watches Dead Letter Queue growth. A steady trickle is normal (broken links exist); a spike means a systemic issue — like a domain now blocking the crawler's IP range.

decisions.title: Frontier queue technology
decisions.rationale: The dominant failure mode in a 5-day, 10B-page crawl isn't total system failure — it's individual fetches timing out against slow or dead servers. SQS gives visibility timeouts, `ApproximateReceiveCount`-driven backoff, and dead-letter routing *for free*. Kafka would require building retry and DLQ semantics by hand on top of consumer offsets, which is exactly the kind of infrastructure work this deadline can't absorb.

decisions.title: Fault-tolerant pipeline shape
decisions.choice: Pipelined stages — fetch, store, enqueue reference, then parse — instead of one monolithic worker
alternatives: A single worker that fetches, parses, and extracts links in one step
decisions.rationale: A monolithic worker means any bug in text extraction forces the *fetch* to be redone too, wasting the exact bandwidth that is this system's scarcest resource (~23K pages/s required). By splitting fetch from parse across two queues, a parser crash only re-runs cheap local computation against HTML that's already safely in blob storage.

decisions.title: Politeness enforcement
decisions.choice: Per-domain Redis lock and sliding-window counter, TTL matched to each domain's Crawl-delay
alternatives: A static delay baked into each worker thread
No cross-worker coordination — rely on queue randomness to spread requests
decisions.rationale: With ~8 fetcher hosts running many threads each, multiple workers can independently dequeue URLs from the same popular domain. A per-thread delay only bounds *that thread's* request rate; it does nothing to stop the fleet collectively exceeding 1 req/s against one domain. Politeness is a property of the whole system, so it needs shared state.

decisions.title: URL dedup fast path
decisions.choice: RedisBloom filter as a pre-check in front of the Metadata DB
alternatives: Query the Metadata DB for every candidate URL
An in-memory hash set per worker
decisions.rationale: At 10B+ discovered link candidates, hitting DynamoDB for every single one to ask 'have we seen this?' would dominate the DB's read capacity. A Bloom filter answers 'definitely new' in O(1) from memory and rejects the vast majority of candidates — mostly re-discovered links to already-crawled pages — without a network round trip. The DB is only consulted on the rare positive match, where its false-positive tolerance costs nothing but an extra read.

decisions.title: Crawler trap prevention
decisions.choice: Max-depth cutoff (15–20 hops from seed), tracked per URL in the Metadata DB
alternatives: Unbounded depth, relying solely on URL-level dedup
A fixed total crawl-time budget with no per-branch limit
decisions.rationale: Session IDs, calendar widgets, and faceted search filters generate effectively infinite *unique* URLs down a single path — URL dedup alone never triggers because every link really is new. Tracking depth from the nearest seed and cutting off a branch past a threshold bounds the worst case cheaply, without needing to detect the trap pattern itself.

decisions.title: Storage split: raw HTML vs. extracted text
decisions.choice: Two separate blob storage locations — raw HTML and clean text
alternatives: A single blob per URL containing both
Discard raw HTML immediately after parsing to save space
decisions.rationale: Storage is cheap; the ~2MB average page fetched over the wire is the expensive resource. Keeping raw HTML around means text-extraction logic can be improved and re-run against the entire 10B-page corpus later without re-crawling a single URL — a rebuild that would otherwise cost another 5-day crawl.

bottlenecks.title: DNS resolution bottleneck
bottlenecks.problem: DNS lookups have historically consumed up to 70% of a naive crawler thread's elapsed time, since every new domain requires a fresh resolution before the first byte can be fetched.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Each fetcher host maintains a local DNS cache, and lookups are round-robined across multiple upstream resolvers so no single resolver becomes the fleet's shared chokepoint.

bottlenecks.title: Frontier queue thundering herd on a popular domain
bottlenecks.problem: Many pages across the web link to the same large domain (e.g. a major news site), so a burst of same-domain URLs can land in the Frontier Queue together and race for the same per-domain lock in the Rate Limiter.
bottlenecks.mitigation: The Rate Limiter defers contended fetches via SQS's `ChangeMessageVisibility`, with jitter added to the delay so deferred workers don't all retry in the same instant and re-create the collision.

bottlenecks.title: Crawler traps / infinite link mazes
bottlenecks.problem: Dynamically generated pages — calendar widgets, session-id-bearing links, faceted search — can produce an effectively unbounded number of unique URLs down a single branch, each one passing URL-level dedup because it genuinely is new.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Every URL carries a depth value in the Metadata DB. Branches past 15–20 hops from the nearest seed are simply never enqueued, bounding the worst case without needing to detect the trap pattern itself.

bottlenecks.title: Parser falling behind fetchers
bottlenecks.problem: Fetching is I/O-bound and cheap to parallelize; parsing is CPU-heavier. If the parser fleet can't keep pace, the Further Processing Queue backs up and raw HTML accumulates in blob storage faster than it's consumed.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Parser workers autoscale directly on Further Processing Queue depth rather than running a fixed fleet size, so parse capacity grows automatically under sustained fetch pressure.

bottlenecks.title: Metadata DB hot keys from popular domains
bottlenecks.problem: Every fetch against a popular domain would otherwise trigger a robots.txt / crawl-delay lookup against the same Domain table row, concentrating read load on a handful of partition keys.
bottlenecks.mitigation: The Rate Limiter caches each domain's robots.txt rules and crawl-delay in Redis with a periodic refresh, so the hot read path never touches the Metadata DB per-request.

quiz.question: Why does the fetcher put only a reference on the Further Processing Queue instead of the HTML itself?
quiz.answer: SQS messages are capped well below the ~2MB average page size, so the HTML physically couldn't fit. More fundamentally, it decouples the fetch and parse tiers — the queue only needs to carry enough information to locate the page in blob storage, letting each tier scale on its own workload rather than on message size.

quiz.question: Why is a per-domain lock in Redis necessary if the Frontier Queue already spreads work across many fetcher workers?
quiz.answer: The Frontier Queue guarantees fair distribution of *work*, not coordination between workers about *which domain* they're each about to hit. Two workers can independently dequeue URLs for the same domain at the same moment with no shared state. Only a centralized lock — shared across the whole fleet — can enforce a single 1 req/s ceiling per domain.

quiz.question: What happens if a fetcher crashes right after writing HTML to blob storage but before enqueueing the Further Processing Queue reference?
quiz.answer: Nothing is lost. The Frontier Queue message for that URL was never deleted, so its visibility timeout eventually expires and another worker retries the fetch. The redundant write to blob storage is harmless because storage writes are idempotent — the retry simply overwrites the same object.

quiz.question: Why use a Bloom filter for URL dedup instead of just querying the Metadata DB every time?
quiz.answer: At the scale of 10B+ discovered link candidates, a DB read per candidate would overwhelm the Metadata DB's read capacity. A Bloom filter answers 'definitely not seen' from memory in O(1), rejecting most candidates without a network call. Its false positives — rare, tunable — only cost an extra DB check, never a missed page.

quiz.question: Why track 'depth from seed' per URL instead of relying purely on URL-level deduplication to stop infinite crawls?
quiz.answer: Crawler traps like session-ID links or calendar widgets generate URLs that are each genuinely unique, so URL-level dedup never rejects them — there's no duplicate to catch. Depth tracking bounds the damage structurally: once a branch is 15–20 hops from any seed, it's abandoned regardless of whether its URLs look new.

quiz.question: Why keep the raw HTML in blob storage after the text has already been extracted?
quiz.answer: Text extraction logic will improve over time, and re-running it against 10B stored HTML pages is far cheaper than re-fetching them — fetching is bandwidth-bound and takes days, while re-parsing stored HTML is local compute. Bandwidth, not storage, is this system's scarce resource.

quiz.question: Why is 1 request/second per domain a meaningfully different constraint than the system's overall ~23K pages/sec throughput target?
quiz.answer: The overall throughput target is an aggregate across millions of independent domains, while the politeness limit is a ceiling on any *single* domain. The system hits its 23K pages/sec goal through breadth — crawling thousands of domains concurrently — never by exceeding the per-domain limit on any one of them.

summary:
### Architecture Overview

This design models a distributed web crawler that discovers, fetches, and extracts text from 10 billion pages in under 5 days, without losing progress and without overloading the servers it crawls.

### Key Design Principles

**Pipelined stages, not a monolithic worker.** Fetching and parsing are split across two queues — the Frontier Queue and the Further Processing Queue — so a failure or slowdown in one stage never forces redoing the other. Fetching is I/O-bound and bandwidth-expensive; parsing is CPU-bound and cheap to redo. Keeping them independent lets each scale on its own bottleneck.

**Politeness is a shared, not per-worker, constraint.** A Redis-backed per-domain lock and sliding-window counter ensure the *entire fleet* — not just one thread — respects each domain's crawl-delay. Robots.txt rules are cached in the same layer so the hot path never blocks on a database read.

**Two-tier deduplication.** A Bloom filter rejects the overwhelming majority of already-seen URLs in O(1) before they ever reach the Metadata DB, while a content hash computed after each fetch catches pages that are byte-identical under different URLs — mirrors, tracking-parameter variants, and syndicated content.

**The frontier is a loop, not a line.** New URLs discovered during parsing flow back through the Dedup Filter and re-enter the Frontier Queue, expanding the crawl outward from the original seed list until either the frontier drains or the 5-day budget runs out.

**Storage is split by purpose.** Raw HTML and extracted text live in separate locations. Keeping the raw HTML means extraction logic can be improved and re-run against the whole corpus later without re-paying the bandwidth cost of re-fetching 10 billion pages.

### Fault Tolerance

- **Fetcher crash mid-fetch:** the Frontier Queue message's visibility timeout expires and another worker retries automatically — no operator intervention needed.
- **Persistently broken URLs:** after 5 failed attempts (tracked via `ApproximateReceiveCount`), messages move to a Dead Letter Queue instead of retrying forever.
- **Parser backlog:** the parser fleet autoscales directly on Further Processing Queue depth, so a burst of fetched pages doesn't stall the pipeline.
- **Domain-level abuse:** the Politeness Rate Limiter's shared lock prevents the fleet from ever exceeding a domain's crawl-delay, even under retry storms.
